title: Guy de Maupassant, The Necklace recast
author: tbr
note: One borrowed night of glitter; a decade to learn it was paste. After Maupassant, The Necklace, 1884.

scenes.title: The gala
scenes.reentry: Mathilde Loisel believed she had been born for better rooms.

breaths.text: Mathilde Loisel believed she had been born for better rooms.
She lived with her husband, a city clerk in a municipal office near Queens Boulevard, in a walk-up that smelled of radiator dust and takeout containers rinsed for reuse.
She hated the cracked laminate, the fluorescent kitchen, the way their acquaintances posted dinners she could not afford and apartments with plants that looked watered by someone paid to care.
When an invitation came—an industry gala at a Midtown hotel, her husband's office allotted two seats—she wept, not from joy.
"I have nothing to wear," she said, turning the envelope over as if a dress might fall out.
He gave her the money he had saved for a used scooter that would have shortened his commute.
She bought a dress the color of wet ink and stood before the mirror until she almost believed she was someone else.
Still she touched her bare throat and felt unfinished.
She went to Madame Forestier, an old school friend with a doorman building and jewelry that lived in velvet.
"Lend me something," Mathilde said, trying to sound casual, as if borrowing beauty were ordinary.
Forestier opened a box.
Bracelets.
A thin gold chain.
Then Mathilde's fingers stopped on a diamond necklace that caught every lamp in the room.
She fastened it with shaking hands and left before gratitude could become honesty about how much she needed to be seen.
At the gala she was noticed.
Men asked her name as if it mattered.
Women watched her throat.
She danced until her feet hurt inside rented shoes and forgot, for a few hours, the walk-up and the clerk's careful budget and the way desire had always made her mean to herself.
In the cab home she laughed against her husband's shoulder, the city sliding by in wet streaks.
Then, in the fluorescent lobby of their building, beneath a notice about package theft, she put her hand to her neck and found only skin.
They searched the cab company's lost-and-found, the hotel carpet near the ballroom doors, the sidewalk where the doorman swore he had seen nothing.
Nothing.
They told Forestier the clasp had broken and needed repair; Mathilde could not bear to say lost.
They borrowed from a cousin, financed through a storefront lender, signed papers that tasted like metal.
They bought a necklace that matched—or nearly matched—in a bright shop where the salesman spoke softly of clarity and cut.
They returned it in a box that felt heavier than the debt.
Then the years began.
Mathilde dismissed any thought of help she could not pay for.
She scrubbed the building stairs for a reduction in rent.
She took night shifts folding linen in a hotel basement where the air was always damp and the fluorescents never fully died.
Her husband worked overtime until his handwriting slanted with fatigue and his jokes stopped.
They moved to a cheaper unit with a view of a brick wall.
Her voice roughened.
Her beauty—once her only inheritance—went thin and practical, hair tied back, hands red at the knuckles.

Sometimes, walking home at 2 a.m. past a shared scooter tipped on its side, she remembered the weight of diamonds against her collarbone and felt sick with wanting and with the knowledge of what wanting had cost.
Ten years.
The debt died at last, paid to its final ugly cent.
Mathilde's face had learned what work writes on a person.
One Sunday on the river path she saw Madame Forestier, still young-looking, still easy in her coat, holding a coffee.
Mathilde stopped her.
Pride, or what was left of it, made her tell the story: the loss, the replacement, the decade of stairs and linen and silence at dinner.
Forestier took her hands.
Her eyes were strange—soft, almost frightened.
"Oh, my poor Mathilde," she said.
"Mine was paste.
It was worth at most five hundred dollars."
The path kept moving around them—joggers, a dog shaking river water onto the boards, a child with a bright cup.
Mathilde stood there and felt the years rearrange themselves behind her, glittering and worthless, impossible to put back on, impossible even to hate cleanly.
